section.title: Woe to Assyria
section.sectionRationale: This movement pivots from Israel's own guilt to the instrument of that guilt's punishment: Assyria, the rod of God's anger, which oversteps its assigned role and boasts of its own strength, inviting judgment in turn. The oracle closes with an axe felling the mighty forest of Assyria's pride, directly setting up the next movement's shoot rising from a very different stump.
section.thesis: Assyria is genuinely God's chosen instrument of discipline against a godless nation, yet because it arrogantly credits its conquests to its own strength rather than acknowledging the hand that wields it, the LORD will in turn judge Assyria's pride, felling its forest of power the very way an axe fells trees, while a remnant of His own people learns to lean not on their oppressor but on the LORD alone.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Assyria named as the rod of God's anger against a godless nation; Assyria's arrogant boast exposed as mere tool mistaking itself for the wielder; the promised remnant who will finally rely on the LORD alone; and the felling of Assyria's mighty forest of pride.

units.label: The rod of My anger
units.note: Assyria sent against a godless nation

verses.text: Woe to Assyria, the {{shevet|rod}} of My anger; the staff in their hands is My wrath.
I will send him against a godless nation; I will dispatch him against a people destined for My rage, to take spoils and seize plunder, and to trample them down like clay in the streets.
But this is not his intention; this is not his plan. For it is in his heart to destroy and cut off many nations.

units.label: The axe boasting over the one who swings it

verses.text: “Are not all my commanders kings?” he says.
“Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus?
As my hand seized the idolatrous kingdoms whose images surpassed those of Jerusalem and Samaria,
and as I have done to Samaria and its idols, will I not also do to Jerusalem and her idols?”
So when the Lord has completed all His work against Mount Zion and Jerusalem, He will say, “I will punish the king of Assyria for the fruit of his arrogant heart and the proud look in his eyes.
My hand reached as into a nest to seize the wealth of the nations. Like one gathering abandoned eggs, I gathered all the earth. No wing fluttered, no beak opened or chirped.’”
Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it? Does a saw boast over him who saws with it? It would be like a rod waving the one who lifts it, or a staff lifting him who is not wood!

units.label: A remnant will truly rely on the LORD
units.note: not on him who struck them

verses.text: Therefore the Lord GOD of Hosts will send a wasting disease among Assyria's stout warriors, and under his pomp will be kindled a fire like a burning flame.
And the Light of Israel will become a fire, and its Holy One a flame. In a single day it will burn and devour Assyria's thorns and thistles.
The splendor of its forests and orchards, both soul and body, it will completely destroy, as a sickness consumes a man.
The remaining trees of its forests will be so few that a child could count them.
On that day the remnant of Israel and the survivors of the house of Jacob will no longer depend on him who struck them, but they will truly rely on the LORD, the {{qadosh3|Holy One}} of Israel.
A {{shear|remnant}} will return, a remnant of Jacob, to the Mighty God.
Though your people, O Israel, be like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return. Destruction has been decreed, overflowing with righteousness.
For the Lord GOD of Hosts will carry out the destruction decreed upon the whole land.

Therefore this is what the Lord GOD of Hosts says: 
“O My people who dwell in Zion, do not fear Assyria, who strikes you with a rod and lifts his staff against you 
as the Egyptians did.

For in just a little while My fury against you will subside, 
and My anger will turn to their destruction.”
And the LORD of Hosts will brandish a whip against them, as when He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. He will raise His staff over the sea, as He did in Egypt.
On that day the burden will be lifted from your shoulders, and the yoke from your neck. The yoke will be broken because your neck will be too large.

units.label: The mighty forest felled
units.note: Lebanon falls before the Mighty One

verses.text:
Assyria has entered Aiath and passed through Migron, 
storing their supplies at Michmash.
They have crossed at the ford: “We will spend the night at Geba.” Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul flees.

Cry aloud, O Daughter of Gallim! Listen, O Laishah! 
O wretched Anathoth!
Madmenah flees; the people of Gebim take refuge.

Yet today they will halt at Nob, shaking a fist at the mount of Daughter Zion, 
at the hill of Jerusalem.
Behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts will lop off the branches with terrifying power. The tall trees will be cut down, the lofty ones will be felled.
He will clear the forest thickets with an axe, and Lebanon will fall before the Mighty One.

shevet.gloss: Rod, staff, scepter, an instrument of both discipline and rule. Assyria is genuinely the shevet, rod, of God's anger, a real, appointed instrument of divine judgment, yet an instrument remains only that, never the one who wields it, the very point Assyria's pride refuses to acknowledge.

qadosh3.gloss: Holy, set apart. The Holy One of Israel, Isaiah's favorite divine title, appears here as the one the remnant will finally, truly rely on rather than the foreign power that struck them, holiness and covenant faithfulness held together in a single name.

shear.gloss: Remnant, that which remains. This is the same root behind the name of Isaiah's first son, Shear-jashub, a remnant will return, Isaiah 7:3, tying this oracle's promise directly back to the sign given years earlier to faithless Ahaz.

basic.context: God openly calls Assyria His rod, a real and appointed instrument to discipline a godless people, yet Assyria's own ambitions go far beyond merely executing that assignment, boasting arrogantly that its conquests prove its own strength and wisdom rather than acknowledging the God who wielded it all along. Because of that pride, the LORD promises to judge Assyria in turn, felling its mighty forest of power, while a genuine remnant of Israel finally learns to rely not on the very oppressor who struck them but on the LORD alone.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage teaches real, dual accountability: God can genuinely use an evil, pagan empire as His instrument of discipline while still holding that empire fully responsible for its own arrogance and cruelty, since intending evil and being sovereignly used for a limited disciplinary purpose are not the same thing. The uncomfortable question this raises, how God can judge Assyria for doing what He sent it to do, is answered by the axe-and-woodsman image: an instrument overstepping its assigned, limited role into self-glorifying destruction incurs its own guilt, distinct from the purpose for which it was sent.
basic.originalLanguages: Assyria is called God's shevet, rod, a genuine instrument of discipline, yet an instrument that never becomes the wielder. The promised remnant, shear, a term echoing the name of Isaiah's own son Shear-jashub from chapter 7, will finally rely on the qadosh, Holy One, of Israel rather than the power that struck them.
basic.typology: The image of an axe unable to boast over the one who swings it anticipates Paul's language in Romans 9:20-21 of the potter and the clay, creatures who cannot rightly claim independence from or superiority to their maker. The felling of Assyria's mighty forest of pride directly sets up the following chapter's contrasting image of a tender shoot rising from a humble stump, showing that God's kingdom advances not through imperial might but through humble, Spirit-empowered growth.
basic.christ: The remnant who learns to rely wholly on the LORD rather than any human power anticipates the true, faithful Israel embodied fully in Christ, who alone perfectly trusted the Father rather than worldly strength, and who calls His people to the same reliance. The felling of Assyria's proud forest, making way afterward for a humble shoot from a stump, Isaiah 11:1, previews the pattern of the gospel itself, where God's power is displayed not in worldly grandeur but through apparent weakness, culminating in the cross.
basic.god: God is sovereign over every empire, able to summon even a cruel pagan power as His own disciplinary instrument without becoming complicit in that power's independent arrogance or cruelty. He disciplines His own people through real historical suffering, yet He remains committed to preserving and eventually vindicating a faithful remnant, showing that His judgment always serves His larger redemptive purposes rather than final abandonment.
basic.crossReferences: Habakkuk 1:5-11 wrestles with the same tension, God raising up a fierce, wicked nation, Babylon, as an instrument of judgment, then holding that nation accountable in turn. Romans 9:20-21 develops the potter-and-clay image of a creature's proper place before its maker, echoing this chapter's axe-and-woodsman logic. 2 Kings 19:35-37 narrates the actual historical defeat of Sennacherib's Assyrian army outside Jerusalem, a partial, historical fulfillment of this oracle's promised judgment. Isaiah 11:1 immediately follows with the shoot from the stump of Jesse, directly continuing this chapter's felled-forest imagery.
basic.oneStory: This oracle shows that God can use even history's most brutal powers for His own disciplinary purposes without excusing their pride or cruelty, and that His ultimate purpose is not the empire's glory but the survival and true reliance of a faithful remnant. That remnant theme threads directly into the next movement, where a humble shoot rises from what looks like a felled and finished stump, God's pattern of bringing life out of apparent devastation.

context.literary:
The oracle is a long poem with a plain logic, and it is easiest to follow if you notice who is speaking in each stretch. In verses 5 to 7 God speaks about Assyria; in verses 8 to 11 Assyria speaks, quoted at length in its own words; in verse 12 God speaks again and quotes the same speech back in judgment, 'For he says...' in verse 13. The Assyrian king is given the stage and then answered. Verses 16 to 19 turn to fire and forest, verses 20 to 23 to the remnant, verses 24 to 27 to a direct word of comfort to Zion, and verses 28 to 34 to a march and a felling.

The poem begins with a woe and ends with a felling. In between, the pictures of wood run through it like a grain. Assyria is a rod and a staff, wood in a hand, verse 5. The proud king's tools are an axe and a saw, verse 15. The forest burns in verses 17 to 19, thorns and thistles first, then 'the splendor of its forests and orchards.' The final lines bring the axe in again, 'He will clear the forest thickets with an axe, and Lebanon will fall,' verse 34. The wooden tool that thought it was a lord ends as timber in the fire.

The poem pulls two old threads together. Verses 24 to 27 recall the exodus and Midian, so the tormentor of Zion is placed among Pharaoh and Midian's raiders. Verses 28 to 32 are among the most vivid in the book: a dozen place names in a stride, each one a few miles closer to Jerusalem, until the army stops at Nob and 'shakes a fist at the mount of Daughter Zion.' The sudden shift from the list of villages to the verdict in verse 33, 'Behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts will lop off the branches,' is dramatic: the whole march stops in one sentence.

The passage follows directly from the poem of 9:8 to 10:4, where the same hand was upraised against Israel. It shows the One who raised it to be holding something in His hand, and it asks what becomes of the tool when the work is done. The answer is carried over into chapter 11, where a shoot rises from the stump after the forest has been cut.
context.historical:
In the second half of the eighth century BC Assyria was the most formidable power the world had seen. Its kings campaigned almost every year, took tribute where cities submitted, and where they resisted, destroyed them and moved the populations to distant lands. The king's boasts in verses 8 to 14 have an authentic ring. Assyrian royal inscriptions speak of the king in the first person, listing cities taken and rulers made servants, and they often claim that the king's own power, or the power of the god Ashur, has done it. Isaiah is quoting the style of Assyrian propaganda back at it.

The cities listed in verses 9 to 11 are real conquests, and the order in which the king recites them carries a taunt. Damascus fell to Tiglath-pileser in 732 BC, when Ahaz had sent silver and gold from the temple asking for help, 2 Kings 16:7-9. Samaria fell in 722. Hamath and Carchemish fell to Sargon II in the years that followed. The boast has the logic of a conqueror who points to the gods of fallen cities and concludes that Jerusalem's God is no different. That is how the Assyrian field commander argues to the people on the wall in Isaiah 36:18-20: 'Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad?'

The reference to Jerusalem's idols in verses 10 and 11 shows how much the Assyrian misread what he faced. He assumed that a city under a God who could not be seen was one more image to knock down. Isaiah has been saying for chapters that Judah's real problem is its own sin, and the oracle does not deny that Assyria is God's instrument against it.

The march in verses 28 to 32 is a puzzle. It names towns north of Jerusalem in Benjamin, along a ridge route, and brings the army to Nob, a short distance from the city. Sennacherib's campaign in 701 BC came up from the coast through Lachish, 2 Kings 18:13-14. The poem may picture an earlier threat, or it may be a prophetic vision of an approach that did not take the exact historical path. What is certain is that in the end Jerusalem was not taken, and that 'the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men,' Isaiah 37:36, after which Sennacherib went home, and some years later was killed by his own sons, Isaiah 37:37-38.
context.canonical:
The oracle sits in a long line of Scripture about the relation of God's rule to the rulers of the nations. Genesis 50:20 states it in a single sentence: 'what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good.' Pharaoh in Exodus 9:16 is raised up so that God's power might be shown, and yet he is judged for his hardness. The Psalms put the idea in a line, 'Even the wrath of man shall praise You,' Psalm 76:10. Isaiah himself returns to Assyria again and again: God will 'break Assyria in My land,' and take the yoke from His people's shoulders, Isaiah 14:24-27, and Assyria will 'fall, but not by the sword of man,' Isaiah 31:8-9.

The instrument-then-judgment pattern is repeated with Babylon. In Jeremiah God calls Nebuchadnezzar His servant and then says that Babylon's own turn will come, Jeremiah 25:9-12. Habakkuk, who asks how a holy God can use the wicked Chaldeans, receives the answer that they are raised up by God and yet are condemned, 'Because you have plundered many nations, the remnant of the people will plunder you,' Habakkuk 2:8. Zechariah 1:15 gives the divine verdict on nations that overreached: 'I was a little angry, but they have added to the calamity.' The Revelation applies the same pattern to the last empire, where the beast and its kings are moved to carry out God's purpose against Babylon, and then Babylon is thrown down like a millstone into the sea, Revelation 17:16-17 and 18:21.

The remnant theme is equally deep. The name Shear-jashub, 'a remnant will return,' was given to Isaiah's own son, Isaiah 7:3, and Isaiah 1:9 says that only a few survivors kept Judah from being like Sodom. Paul quotes Isaiah 10:22-23 in Romans 9:27-28 to explain that Israel's unbelief does not make God's word fail, and he adds that 'at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace,' Romans 11:5.

The highest case of the principle is the cross. Peter says that Jesus 'was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' and that it was 'you, by the hands of the lawless' who put Him to death, Acts 2:23. The prayer of the church in Acts 4:27-28 says that Herod and Pilate carried out 'what Your hand and will had decided beforehand.' The oracle against Assyria is one of the best-known texts that shows how both could be true.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah spoke to people who were frightened of Assyria and tempted to explain its power in one of two wrong ways. One was to say that Assyria was simply stronger than the God of Judah, which is the conclusion the Assyrian king himself drew. The other was to say that because Assyria was only a tool, it could not be blamed for what it did. Isaiah rejects both. The empire is a tool in God's hand, and the hand is not weak. Yet the tool has a heart, and the heart is proud.

He wanted Judah to understand its situation correctly. The pressure they felt was God's discipline, so Assyria was not the final word about their future. Because He had raised Assyria, He could set a limit on it, and the message of 10:25, 'in just a little while My fury against you will subside,' gives the people the time-frame in which to hope. 'Do not fear Assyria' is the practical purpose of the poem.

He also meant the hearers to see what God thinks of pride. The king does not claim to be God, but he takes the credit that belongs to God. Isaiah's picture of an axe boasting over the woodcutter makes the claim absurd. In the same way, rulers in Judah who trusted political schemes rather than the LORD were being shown that no human wisdom or strength has independent standing.

Finally, he wanted a remnant to hear that its trust must change. Verse 20 says that those who survive will 'no longer depend on him who struck them.' Judah's reliance on Assyria, which Ahaz had practised, was the sin that this judgment would end. The people were to move from leaning on the empire to leaning on the Holy One.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what God did with Assyria and what Assyria thought it was doing. It does not tell later believers that every dominant nation is God's chosen instrument, or that its victories are signs of His approval. The oracle is a specific word about a specific empire in a specific crisis. Treating a modern power as 'the rod of God' is going beyond the text, and Isaiah's own method warns against it: the rod is called a rod because God said so, through a prophet, and not because of what the empire accomplished.

What the text does prescribe by example is a posture toward powers. Do not fear them, verse 24. Do not lean on them, verse 20. Do not imitate them in pride, verses 12 to 15. The 'do not fear' applies in the church's life under hostile governments, as Paul's reading of rulers in Romans 13 and the martyrs' trust in Revelation 13 show, even where the particular rulers are plainly unjust.

The passage also provides a pattern for how to read evil that happens to God's people. Habakkuk and Jeremiah are filled with this question, and the cross answers it most deeply. The believer can be sure that no evil falls outside God's governing hand, and equally sure that those who do it are responsible for it. This guards against fatalism on one side, where we say nothing can be done, and against blaming God for what others do, on the other. Joseph's words in Genesis 50:20 are the model.

debates.question: How can God justly judge Assyria for doing exactly what He sent it to do?

views.label: Assyria exceeded its assigned, limited role
views.case: God sent Assyria against a specific nation for a specific purpose, but Assyria's own intention, verse 7, was 'to destroy and cut off many nations.' The commission was limited and the conquest was not. Zechariah 1:15 says the same of other nations: 'I was a little angry, but they have added to the calamity.'

views.label: The motive and manner of the instrument matter
views.case: Even if Assyria had stayed within the commission, its heart was proud: 'By the strength of my hand I have done this, and by my wisdom,' verse 13. The guilt is in what the heart claims, in the credit it takes and the cruelty it enjoys, and it is distinct from the purpose the action unknowingly served.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that being used in God's purposes never removes an agent's own responsibility. This is how Scripture handles Pharaoh, Babylon and the men who crucified Jesus, Acts 2:23, and it asks readers to hold the sovereignty and the accountability together without making one swallow the other.

debates.question: What is the march of verses 28 to 32: a historical advance, a literary picture, or a prophetic vision of a future threat?

views.label: An actual advance, probably early in Isaiah's ministry
views.case: The towns are real and lie in an order that makes sense on the roads north of Jerusalem, and the closing 'Yet today they will halt at Nob' reads like an eyewitness report. Some link it to the Assyrian pressure of the 730s when Judah was under threat, others to a march before Sennacherib's campaign.

views.label: A vision of Sennacherib's coming
views.case: Because the oracle ends with Assyria's downfall, many place it in 701 BC. The difficulty is that Sennacherib came up from the southwest through Lachish, 2 Kings 18:13-14, not from the north, so this view treats the route as a poetic heightening rather than a report.

views.label: A prophetic picture that is not tied to one route
views.case: The list may be a rhetorical device that puts a terror in the hearer's ear as the names come faster, in the manner of a lament, with no claim to describe the precise path of any one army. What matters is that the advance stops at Jerusalem's edge.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle which campaign Isaiah has in mind, and the main point is the same on each reading: the army that has swept through every village stops at the mount of Zion, and God, not the city's defenders, breaks it.

debates.question: Who or what is the forest felled in verses 33 and 34?

views.label: Assyria's army and leaders
views.case: The verses follow verses 16 to 19, where Assyria's forest burns and so few trees are left that a child could count them. Ezekiel 31:3 calls Assyria 'a cedar in Lebanon,' and Isaiah's own taunt of the Assyrian king in Isaiah 37:24 uses the same pictures of tall cedars. The tall trees cut down are the Assyrian host and its commanders.

views.label: The proud of Judah, or the Davidic line itself
views.case: A few interpreters read the felling as including Judah's own proud leaders, in the way that Isaiah 2:12-13 sets the day of the LORD against 'all the cedars of Lebanon, lofty and lifted up.' Others link the felled tree to the stump of Jesse that follows in 11:1, suggesting that the line of David is itself cut down before a shoot rises.

debates.bearing: The immediate setting favours Assyria, since the speech of the proud king and the burning forest of verses 16 to 19 lead straight to it. Isaiah's wider teaching is that pride of every sort is cut down, so the other reading is not foreign to the book, and the move to the stump in 11:1 shows that one felling leads to another.

study.originalLanguages:
The oracle's central tool, the 'rod,' is shevet, and its partner 'staff,' verse 5, is matteh. These are everyday objects with a long history in Scripture. The shevet is the shepherd's rod, the king's sceptre and the father's discipline: in 2 Samuel 7:14 God says of David's son, 'I will discipline him with the rod of men.' To call Assyria the rod of God's anger is to say that it is wielded with a parent's purpose, to correct, even though the one holding the rod is a stranger. The same word returns in Isaiah 11:4 for 'the rod of His mouth,' the rod of the righteous King, which makes the rod of 10:5 a poor shadow of what is coming.

The word for what drives the rod is za'am, 'indignation' or 'wrath.' It frames the passage: the rod's staff is God's za'am in verse 5, and in verse 25 God says that 'in just a little while' His za'am against Zion will 'subside.' The same wrath that was handed to the empire is called back. A wrath with a start and a finish is a disciplinary wrath, and verse 25 says its limit is already fixed.

The verses about yoke and burden pick up a vocabulary from chapter 9. In 9:4 the LORD shatters 'the yoke of their burden, the bar across their shoulders,' and in 10:27 'the burden will be lifted from your shoulders, and the yoke from your neck.' The word for yoke, ol, comes a third time in Isaiah 14:25, where God will take Assyria's yoke off His people. Shoulder, shekhem, gathers the pictures: the burden is lifted from Israel's shoulder, and in 9:6 the government rests on the child's shoulder. The relief of the people and the rule of the King are the same event seen from two sides.

Assyria's 'glory,' kavod, is what God burns. In verse 16 the fire is kindled 'under his pomp,' and in verse 18 the 'splendor' of the forest is destroyed. Kavod means weight, and the weighty things of a boastful empire are fuel. By contrast, Israel's God is 'the Light of Israel' in verse 17, the same word for light as the great light of 9:2. The light that rises on the dark land is also a fire that burns the thorn and the thistle, and the pair of thorns and thistles (shamir and shayit) recalls their use in 9:18 for the fire of Israel's own wickedness.

The remnant 'will truly rely' in verse 20, using the verb shaan, 'lean on.' A staff is something one leans on, so the verb is chosen with care: they will no longer lean on the staff of Assyria, and they will lean on the LORD 'in truth.' The same verb appears when Egypt is called 'that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it,' Isaiah 36:6. Leaning on a human power is always leaning on a reed.

In verse 21 the verb of the remnant's return is shuv, 'turn' or 'return.' The Septuagint translates the sentence in verse 22 with a verb meaning 'will be saved,' and that is the form Paul quotes, 'only the remnant will be saved,' Romans 9:27. The two words belong together in Isaiah: to turn back to the LORD is to be saved. Paul's use of the Greek shows how the first translators heard the Hebrew, not merely as a physical return to the land but as deliverance.

typology.fulfillment: An empire raised to discipline a people and then answered for its pride becomes the pattern for every later power that God uses and judges. Babylon plays the role in Habakkuk and Jeremiah, and in Revelation the final city is both used and thrown down, Revelation 17:16-17 and 18:21. The pattern reaches its decisive form at the cross, where men who acted out of fear and malice did what God's 'hand and will had decided beforehand,' Acts 4:27-28. The type falls short in that Assyria was an unwitting instrument, and Jesus was no passive victim: He laid down His life of His own accord, John 10:18.

The remnant is a small number preserved from judgment who learn to rely on God. It looks forward to the faithful few within Israel in every generation and finally to the people gathered around Christ, whom Paul calls 'a remnant chosen by grace,' Romans 11:5. It is fulfilled in Christ Himself, the faithful One in whom Israel's calling is kept, and in those united to Him. The type falls short because the remnant of Isaiah's day is defined by survival and loyalty, while the remnant of the gospel is defined by grace alone.

typology.type: The yoke lifted from the shoulder, Isaiah 10:27
typology.fulfillment: The yoke of Assyria is broken as Egypt's was, and Isaiah draws the exodus into the picture, verse 26. In Jesus the picture becomes an invitation: 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened... Take My yoke upon you,' Matthew 11:28-30. The escalation is that the oppressor is no longer an army but sin and death, Hebrews 2:14-15. The type falls short because the yoke of Assyria is replaced by freedom from a human ruler, while the yoke of Christ is a gentle service.

typology.type: The Light of Israel as fire, Isaiah 10:17
typology.fulfillment: The Holy One who is light to His people is a flame to those who set themselves against Him. The New Testament carries this over in two ways: Jesus is the light of the world, John 8:12, and 'our God is a consuming fire,' Hebrews 12:29. The fire, in the end, falls on every proud thing, 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8. The type is partial in that Isaiah's fire is a historic defeat of one army, whereas the consuming fire of the last day is final.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ at the cross, and that is where it is most disturbing and most comforting. Assyria's pride was real and its judgment was just, yet God used it. In the death of Jesus the same truth is stated in the highest case. Peter says that Jesus 'was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' and in the same sentence that it was 'you, by the hands of the lawless' who killed Him, Acts 2:23. When Pilate boasts of his authority, Jesus tells him, 'You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed Me over to you is guilty of greater sin,' John 19:10-11. The structure is that of Isaiah 10: a ruler holds power that is given from above, uses it with evil intent, and answers for it. The difference is that the 'rod' is now raised against the Holy One Himself, and God's own purpose of rescue is carried out through it.

It leads to Christ by contrast with pride. The Assyrian says, 'By the strength of my hand I have done this, and by my wisdom,' and 'I gathered all the earth,' verses 13 and 14. In the wilderness the devil showed Jesus 'all the kingdoms of the world and their glory' and offered them without a fight, and Jesus refused, Matthew 4:8-10. The One who is 'existing in the form of God' did not treat equality with God as something to be seized, but 'emptied Himself' and 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death,' Philippians 2:6-8. What the empire grabbed and was cut down for, the Son was given because He did not grab it.

It leads to Christ by the Holy One and the light. In verse 17 the Light of Israel and the Holy One of Israel are one and the same, who becomes fire against the proud. Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and the unclean spirit cries, 'the Holy One of God!' Mark 1:24, and Peter accuses his hearers of rejecting 'the Holy and Righteous One,' Acts 3:14. The New Testament does not hesitate to apply these names to Him. When Isaiah says that the Holy One will become a flame for the proud, he describes the same Person who will come to judge, and who has already borne judgment for those who rely on Him.

It leads to Christ by the remnant and the yoke. The faithful Servant stands as the true remnant of Israel, the one who did lean on the LORD completely. In Him a people are gathered who 'will truly rely on the LORD.' And the yoke lifted from the neck becomes His own call: 'Take My yoke upon you... for My yoke is easy and My burden is light,' Matthew 11:29-30. The final oppressor from whom He frees us is not an empire but sin and death.

Two cautions. First, the passage does not name the Messiah and it is wrong to turn the Assyrian axe or the felled forest into pictures of Jesus. The links are made by the New Testament's own use of the pattern. Second, the felling of Lebanon is not a story about Christ's death, though the shoot that follows in Isaiah 11:1 is. The oracle prepares the ground by clearing it, and the next chapter plants what grows.
study.god:
The first thing the oracle shows about God is the reach of His government. He speaks of Assyria as a tool in His hand, and He says that He will 'send' and 'dispatch' it, verse 6. Nothing about Assyria's rise is outside His rule. This is not a reduced claim about God's involvement but the claim that empires, their kings and the whole course of their campaigns belong to Him, and the God who ordains does so 'long ago,' as He later tells Sennacherib: 'Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it,' Isaiah 37:26.

He is holy, and His holiness does not excuse proud power. The Holy One of Israel is the One the Assyrian has blasphemed, as Isaiah 37:23 will put it, and this is why the tool cannot be innocent. God is not a manager who uses whatever works and passes no judgment on the means. The same God who wields the axe also sits in judgment on the arm that would boast of the cutting. Isaiah says it more sharply than anyone: 'Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it?' In the poem's logic, pride is not only a moral failing but a fundamental mistake about who God is.

He judges with order and begins at home. Verse 12 says that the LORD completes 'all His work against Mount Zion and Jerusalem' before He turns on Assyria. Isaiah elsewhere calls this judgment His 'strange work,' Isaiah 28:21, and Peter says that 'it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God,' 1 Peter 4:17. God does not exempt His people from the standards He holds the nations to. Neither does He abandon them to the rod: the discipline has a limit, and the limit is part of His design.

He is faithful to a remnant. The sentence on the nation is 'overflowing with righteousness,' verse 22, but the very same verse says a remnant will return. God preserves a people through judgment, and in verse 21 the remnant returns to 'the Mighty God,' El Gibbor, whose title the Child of 9:6 will also bear. He does not judge to be rid of a people but to bring a few back, to Himself.

He tells the frightened not to be afraid, and gives them a reason. 'O My people who dwell in Zion, do not fear Assyria,' verse 24, is spoken to people with real reasons for fear, who were being struck with the rod. The ground of the comfort is not that the danger is small but that God's anger will turn: it is a limit already set. He appeals to what He has done before, 'as when He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb,' and 'as He did in Egypt,' verse 26. God rests His present promises on His past acts.

There is a tension the passage does not hide, and Habakkuk will feel it: how can eyes 'too pure to look upon evil' use a wicked nation to do His work, Habakkuk 1:13? Isaiah does not explain the mechanism. He gives the two truths and leaves them together. For worship, the oracle teaches us to bow to a God who holds history and is not implicated in its evil, to refuse to lean on any power that is only a rod, and to take comfort that every tyrant's hour has a boundary set by the Holy One.

crossReferences.note: The Assyrian field commander's speech to the people on Jerusalem's wall repeats the logic of 10:9-11. He lists the gods of Hamath, Arpad and Samaria and concludes that the LORD cannot save Jerusalem either. Isaiah 10 predicts the arrogance and gives God's verdict before the commander has spoken.

God's answer to Sennacherib, which reads like a reply to the boast of 10:13-14: 'Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it.' What the king took as his own strength was God's plan, and God will put a hook in his nose and send him back the way he came.

The historical outcome. The angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 in the Assyrian camp, Sennacherib withdraws, and he is later killed by his own sons. The great forest of 10:33-34 is felled in one night, and the shaking fist at Zion never closes on it.

Habakkuk faces the same puzzle in the following century: God raises up the Chaldeans, whose strength is their own god. The prophet then protests, Habakkuk 1:13, and receives the same answer as Isaiah 10, that the instrument will answer for its plunder, Habakkuk 2:8.

God says of nations that He was 'a little angry, but they have added to the calamity.' It is a compact summary of Isaiah 10:7: the commission was small and the destruction large, and the extra is charged to the nation's own account.

God promises to discipline David's son 'with the rod of men.' The rod of Isaiah 10:5 belongs in the same family of words, a rod of correction. The point is that discipline from outside is part of a father's dealing, which makes Assyria's rod a sign that God still regards Judah as His own.

God swears that He will 'break Assyria in My land' and remove its yoke from His people's shoulders, in the same vocabulary as 10:27. The passage adds that this is God's plan for the whole earth, 'and who can thwart Him?' It fixes Assyria's end as part of a purpose for every nation.

The flood of the Euphrates, the king of Assyria and all his pomp, sweeps into Judah 'up to the neck.' It is the other side of 10:5-6: Assyria is sent against the godless nation, and the flood reaches Judah too. The following verses of chapter 10 answer by saying how far it may go and when it will stop.

Ezekiel calls Assyria 'a cedar in Lebanon' that towered into the clouds. It supports reading the felled forest of Isaiah 10:33-34 as Assyria, and shows that the prophets used the imagery of a great tree for an empire's pride and its fall.

Paul quotes Isaiah 10:22-23 to explain that Israel's unbelief does not mean God's word has failed, since from the start 'only the remnant will be saved.' The remnant of Isaiah's oracle is the hinge of Paul's argument that God keeps faith with His promise.

The church prays that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the people of Israel did what God's 'hand and will had decided beforehand.' It is the Isaiah 10 principle at the greatest case: real human guilt and a real divine plan, held together without either cancelling the other.

Jesus invites the weary and burdened to take His yoke. Against the background of Isaiah 10:27, where the burden is lifted from the shoulder and the yoke from the neck, His words offer a different kind of freedom, a rest from every tyrant, in the gentle service of the King.

study.oneStory:
This oracle belongs to the part of the Bible's story where God's rule over the whole world is displayed against the empires. From the beginning, power that makes itself the centre of the world is shown to be borrowed. Pharaoh learned it in Egypt, where God raised him up to show His power in him, and Nebuchadnezzar learned it in the field with the beasts, until he acknowledged that 'the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind,' Daniel 4:32. Isaiah's picture of an axe boasting over the woodcutter tells the same story for Assyria, and it reaches back to the first act of pride, in which a creature wanted to be like the Most High, as Isaiah 14:13-14 puts it for the king of Babylon.

The oracle also tells a story of discipline and remnant. Judah has sinned, and God sends a rod. The rod is not allowed to finish the work, and a remnant survives to rely on the LORD. This is the pattern of the exile and return, and of the way God keeps a people alive through every judgment. Isaiah's son Shear-jashub is the walking sign of it, and Paul reads the whole history of Israel in its light, Romans 9 to 11.

After Isaiah the story shows the pattern repeated. Assyria falls to Babylon; Babylon is used against Jerusalem and then is judged in turn; Persia, Greece and Rome follow. The prophets keep saying the same things: God raises, God limits, God judges the proud. The New Testament shows Rome as one more rod, with Pilate holding authority that was 'given from above,' and then shows the empire answering for what it did.

The cross is the place where all these lines meet. The greatest evil, the killing of the Holy One, is done by proud men and is also the plan of God for the world's rescue. After that the rod no longer needs to fall on the believer, who is accepted in Christ, and the remnant becomes a multitude from every nation. The call 'Do not fear' is repeated by Jesus to His disciples as they face the powers of the day.

The end of the story is the end of the proud empires. In Revelation Babylon is cast down like a millstone into the sea, and 'the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ,' Revelation 11:15. Isaiah's felled forest finds its last form there. What stands afterward is not a rod but a King, and the next chapter of Isaiah already points to Him: the shoot rising from the stump of Jesse in Isaiah 11:1 is what the felling makes room for.

quiz.q: In what sense is Assyria called 'the rod of My anger' in verse 5?

options.text: God genuinely appoints and uses Assyria as His instrument of discipline against a godless nation.
options.note: Verse 6 confirms this: God sends Assyria against a people destined for His rage.

options.text: Assyria acts entirely independently, with no relation to God's purposes.
options.note: The text explicitly says God sends and dispatches Assyria for this purpose.

options.text: Assyria is a symbolic figure with no historical referent.
options.note: Assyria is a real, historical empire, not merely a symbolic figure.

options.text: God approves of every intention and action Assyria takes.
options.note: Verse 7 explicitly distinguishes Assyria's own destructive intentions from God's limited, assigned purpose.

quiz.q: What is the point of the illustration in verse 15, 'does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it?'

options.text: An instrument, however powerful, has no right to claim independence from or superiority over the one who wields it.
options.note: This directly rebukes Assyria's arrogant boast of achieving its conquests by its own strength and wisdom.

options.text: It celebrates human tool-making skill in ancient warfare.
options.note: The image functions as a rebuke of pride, not a celebration of craftsmanship.

options.text: It proves that tools are more powerful than the people who use them.
options.note: The image argues the opposite: the tool is entirely subordinate to the one who wields it.

options.text: It describes a literal woodworking accident.
options.note: This is metaphorical language rebuking Assyria's pride, not a literal report of an accident.

quiz.q: What will the surviving remnant of Israel finally do, according to verse 20?

options.text: Truly rely on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, rather than on the very power that struck them.
options.note: This marks a genuine turning point, from dependence on foreign power to dependence on God alone.

options.text: Form a permanent military alliance with Assyria.
options.note: The text explicitly says they will no longer depend on him who struck them, the opposite of an alliance.

options.text: Abandon worship of the LORD entirely.
options.note: The remnant's response is described as increased, genuine reliance on the LORD, not abandonment of Him.

options.text: Return immediately to full national independence and prosperity.
options.note: The emphasis is on spiritual reliance on God, not primarily a claim about immediate political restoration.

quiz.q: What historical event does this oracle's promised judgment on Assyria likely anticipate, at least in part?

options.text: The sudden defeat of Sennacherib's army outside Jerusalem recorded in 2 Kings 19:35-37.
options.note: This dramatic, historically attested event is often read as at least a partial fulfillment of the judgment promised here.

options.text: The fall of Babylon to the Medo-Persians.
options.note: This oracle addresses Assyria specifically, a different empire from Babylon, which Isaiah addresses in other chapters.

options.text: The return from exile under Cyrus.
options.note: That later event involves Babylon and Persia, not the Assyrian judgment in view here.

options.text: The Maccabean revolt against Greek rule.
options.note: That much later event is unrelated to Isaiah's eighth century BC Assyrian oracle.

quiz.q: How does the forest-felling image at the end of chapter 10 connect to chapter 11?

options.text: It directly sets up the contrasting image of a humble shoot rising from the stump of Jesse in the very next verse.
options.note: The mighty forest of Assyria's pride is felled just before Isaiah 11:1 introduces new life from a very different, humble stump.

options.text: It has no relationship to the following chapter's content.
options.note: The imagery deliberately connects, felled forest giving way to a shoot from a stump, contrasting worldly power with humble, divine growth.

options.text: It describes the same shoot mentioned in chapter 11 growing from the same tree.
options.note: The felled forest represents Assyria's proud power, while the stump of Jesse in chapter 11 represents David's humbled line, a deliberate contrast rather than the same image.

options.text: It is a purely agricultural note unrelated to any theological point.
options.note: The imagery carries clear theological weight, contrasting proud imperial power with the humble source of the coming Messiah.

questions: God can use even a cruel, ungodly power for His own purposes without excusing that power's independent sin. Where do you need to trust God's sovereignty over a difficult circumstance or unjust situation you cannot control?
Assyria credited its own strength and wisdom for what God actually accomplished through it. Where are you tempted to take credit for what is really God's provision or working in your life?

The remnant finally learned to rely on the LORD rather than on the power that had struck them. What or who have you been leaning on for security that you need to release in favor of trusting God alone?

God promised the yoke would be lifted because 'your neck will be too large,' a picture of strength given specifically for that burden. Where do you need to trust that God is currently strengthening you for a weight you are still carrying?

The proud forest of Assyria's power gets felled just before a humble shoot rises in the next chapter. Where in your own life might God be clearing away something impressive to make room for something humble but truly life-giving?

translationNotes.note: 'A wasting disease' and 'a fire like a burning flame' may describe both the sudden decimation of Sennacherib's army, 2 Kings 19:35, and function as poetic imagery for total, consuming judgment.
'Destruction has been decreed, overflowing with righteousness' pairs judgment directly with divine righteousness, showing the coming devastation is not arbitrary but a just and measured response.

This vivid list of villages, Aiath, Migron, Michmash, Geba, Ramah, and others, traces a specific invasion route toward Jerusalem from the north, creating a mounting, almost real-time sense of approaching danger before the LORD's sudden intervention.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from the Makor scripture toolkit for Isaiah 10:5-34.
